result.summary: Do not close the design gate: manifest replay can still erase a shelf alias and expose the retained originals to recursive cleanup.

findings.title: Preserve ancestor aliases during symlink replay too
findings.body: Table V exempts `symlink` replay from the ancestor guard, leaving the same evidence-loss problem X19 fixes only inside the disposer. Consider `<state>` → `<claude>/skills/wienerdog-test` → `<core>/logs`, with an original in `logs/quarantine/`. A matching symlink manifest entry resolves above the protected shelf, so X16 permits it. An in-memory probe of the shipped `reverse()` confirmed that it unlinks this entry. The following disposer then encounters a dangling `<state>` alias; X17 reconstructs anchors beneath the lexical state path, and X18 no longer protects `logs` from recursive deletion. Thus the prescribed reverse→dispose sequence can destroy the original. This also applies when the alias is introduced after the gate, within the specification's existing interleaving model.
findings.recommendation: Extend the pre-dispatch guard to preserve symlink entries whose removal would break resolution of a protected shelf, including intermediate aliases. Keep the ordinary `dir` exemption. Add a regression exercising reverse() followed by both disposer calls and a retry, asserting that the alias and original bytes survive.

next_steps: Close the replay alias gap and rerun the design review before implementation.
